canonicalTeaching.requirement: Identity or receptor expression describes a useful product attribute but does not by itself establish tested biological function.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A cell-product lot is checked against specified quality requirements before its disposition. Identity, live-cell measures and biological activity answer different questions about that lot.

Potency is relevant biological activity under defined conditions. FDA's November 2026 guidance aims for every released lot to have the ability to achieve the intended therapeutic effect and expects the relationship between a measured attribute and the product's mechanism of action to be supported by characterisation, nonclinical or clinical studies; where the mechanism is not fully understood, a statistical relationship such as a correlation with outcomes may help. Identity, receptor expression and viability do not establish activity.

canonicalTeaching.requirement: A product-relevant activity comparison needs defined product-plus-target and target-only conditions, background and response controls.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Controls, reference material and handling state. Potency protocols should set predefined sample and system suitability criteria, and a run should be invalidated if system suitability fails. Reference material lots should be qualified and monitored for stability. Release assays must use a sample taken after all manufacturing steps that may affect potency, with cryopreservation named as an example, so a test on fresh material does not stand for the final product.

Method card, what it measures: whether specified effector cells cause death of specified target cells under controlled laboratory conditions, at a stated effector-to-target ratio and time. Readouts: flow cytometry that separates labelled targets from effectors and uses death-associated staining, release assays, or imaging over time. A fall in a metabolic or growth signal can reflect slowed growth and not death, so it needs validation as evidence of killing. Controls: target-only survival wells, effector identification and viability, a positive-control response, irrelevant or antigen-negative targets and suitable antigen or presentation perturbations, plus maximum release where relevant. Failure modes: high spontaneous death, mistaken target identity, aggregates, dye transfer, artificial loading, mismatched ratios or a readout that mainly measures growth.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Direct and surrogate measures. A direct biological assay measures activity such as target-cell killing; a surrogate measures a related attribute and needs a supported link to function. FDA's January 2011 potency guidance (now superseded) used the term assay matrix for complementary tests. The 2026 guidance recommends developing multiple assays that measure potency-related CQAs early, with redundant assays discontinued later. Many unrelated measurements do not add up to potency.

canonicalTeaching.requirement: Potency interpretation and release criteria are product-specific, under stated conditions and references, with no universal passing cutoff implied.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reading a killing result. A figure such as 60 per cent killing is not comparable between laboratories unless target identity, effector-to-target ratio and observation time are stated, and relative potency needs a named reference and model. FDA's CAR T guidance describes orthogonal methods such as a cell-killing assay, transduction efficiency and cytokine measurement. No universal passing cutoff applies across products.

Validation is about the assay, not the drug. The 2026 guidance asks that release assays measure potency with sufficient specificity, accuracy or precision over their reportable range, that performance be established under actual conditions of use, and that phase-appropriate acceptance criteria be set with failing lots rejected. Qualification and validation do not show that a drug improves a clinical endpoint.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Background arithmetic, fictional: matched wells of 100 identifiable targets show 30% death without effectors and 40% with them at the same 2-hour endpoint. Raw death is 40%, but 30% occurs without effectors, so the excess is 40 minus 30 = 10 percentage points. That excess is associated with the tested condition and does not identify which deaths the effectors caused, and calling the result 40% immune killing is not justified. A control-normalised specific-lysis formula gives a different quantity from an excess-death calculation, so the method has to be named, and a high baseline death can make the experiment unsuitable.

Controls: target-only survival wells, effector identification and viability, a positive-control response, irrelevant or antigen-negative targets and suitable antigen or presentation perturbations, plus maximum release where relevant.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Comparable does not mean identical. Q5E says comparability shows that pre-change and post-change product are highly similar and that existing knowledge predicts that any differences have no adverse impact on safety or efficacy. First describe what changed and which properties it might alter, then use methods able to detect those effects. FDA's CAR T guidance says meeting current lot-release criteria is typically insufficient to establish comparability, and Q5E notes that stability studies can reveal subtle differences.

Measurement caution. An assay change can itself create an apparent product difference, which is why FDA's potency guidance has sections on reference materials and on assay changes and transfers. The CAR T guidance asks for predefined acceptance criteria and appropriate statistical methods. A nonsignificant test alone does not establish similarity, because an insensitive comparison can miss an important difference; this is an inference from the need for predefined criteria and sensitive methods.
A process bridge is not head-to-head equivalence between different therapies.
Release of a lot is a quality decision, separate from regulatory authorisation of the product, from a patient's eligibility, and from evidence of clinical benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: After cleavage the crude peptide is a mixture needing purification and characterisation, and the synthesiser's last step is not a release decision. In Truex et al. electrospray mass spectrometry of the unpurified products showed the desired mass as the main product for all 29 test peptides, while purity was measured separately by analytical reverse-phase HPLC at 214 nm, with greater than 95 per cent HPLC purity used as the purity criterion. In that deliberately difficult 29-peptide commercial-vendor comparison, 17 peptides were synthesised, 10 passed after purification, and 7 stayed at 89 to 94 per cent even after two or three rounds. The 95 per cent figure is that paper's criterion, not a clinical-release threshold.

Assay peptides versus the clinical product. The same paper made 15 to 16-mer peptides for immune-assessment assays and longer immunising peptides of up to 30 residues for vaccination, and its authors describe clinical-grade manufacture as something they envision. Making an assay peptide does not show manufacture of a formulated, released vaccine product, and chemical assembly does not select a useful cancer antigen or show benefit. A shorter instrument run does not establish the turnaround of the whole program.
